title: Aerialists float through vibrant skies in Brook Warren’s ongoing performance project
summary: It’s a departure from the photojournalist’s documentary style.
content: A lot of people head into Colorado’s mountains each year to see — and photograph — aspen groves turning yellow and red as winter sets in. The internet is full of images of the natural show, which usually center the colors themselves. But photographer Brooke Warren has taken a different approach to working in the trees, using them instead as a setting for something magical. For the last few years, she’s brought aerial performers into the woods near her home in Ouray, inviting them to spin and float on colorful silk suspended in the exploding color. The results look like something from a fairy tale: human bodies stretched out as if they’re swimming in midair. Courtesy: Brooke Warren Aerial silks in the changing aspens. Oct. 5, 2024. Warren studied photojournalism and said that experience has influenced most of the work she’s done since, from her time working for publications like High Country News, through a decade of commercial gigs and into her current role as a spokesperson for Ouray County. “I always wanted to be a National Geographic photographer or something like that, and I’ve always been really attracted to using the camera as a way to understand other people, other cultures, other experiences,” she said. Ad: But her growing performance portfolio comes from a different place, she said. While her photojournalistic style relies on discovery — learning about people and places as she digs into a project — this work begins with things she knows intimately. Warren is a performer herself, climbing silks for audiences in town a few times a year. And she grew up photographing Colorado’s natural beauty, as a kid in Crested Butte with a botanist mother who used a camera in her work. Courtesy: Brooke Warren Aerial silks in the changing aspens. Oct. 5, 2024. “These aerial photos are driven by my own experience and wanting to share the feeling of what I enjoy in the world with other people,” she said. “It’s an opportunity for me to hone in on an idea and focus on posing a subject, asking them to do things rather than documenting what’s in front of me.” Courtesy: Brooke Warren South Mineral Creek, near Silverton. Sept. 26, 2026. Courtesy: Brooke Warren South Mineral Creek, near Silverton. Sept. 26, 2026. Warren said she loves this practice because it engages both body and mind. Since she’s been trained to float and spin from silks and rings, she knows how to direct her subjects into correct postures and positions, exploring the form itself as she layers performers into Ouray’s autumn landscape. “I’m more influenced by the capturing of a moment, or a peak moment of a dance,” she said. “It’s also the connection that I have with the artist.” Courtesy: Brooke Warren A High Alpine Aerial student flips through the air. April 17, 2025. The connection with that community is huge, she added. This ongoing project is also a way to reinvest in them. “When you get a photo of yourself doing something that you love, there’s a huge boost of confidence and you find a lot of pride in that … I want to offer that to those folks,” she said. “It’s an opportunity for them to feel confident in their bodies and confident in their skill sets and be able to celebrate their own abilities.” Courtesy: Brooke Warren A High Alpine Aerial student flips through the air with Mt. Sneffels in the backdrop. April 17, 2025. Courtesy: Brooke Warren A High Alpine Aerial student levitates with Mt. Sneffels in the backdrop. April 17, 2025. Still, her journalistic impulses are never far away. Warren said she’s been pursuing a documentary project about circus performers on the Western Slope as she works on these more constructed images in the autumn air. You can see more of Warren’s work on her Instagram .

title: Colorado Holiday Lights Map 2026: Where to find the best home light displays in the state
summary: Plot a course to see some of the best holiday lights in the state or submit your display for inclusion on our map!
content: Looking for some of the best holiday light displays in the state? Want to show yours off? We’ve got you covered. Whether Griswoldian or Lilliputian, you can submit a photo and address for inclusion in our new holiday lights map , or use it to plan your family’s holiday decoration driving tour. To be clear, we’re talking about residential lights here. Denver’s famous decorating tradition is great, and all, but it’s not for everyone. There are plenty of lighting-based celebrations of the season put on by towns, attractions and other pros — we have a list of them here — but this map is for us regular Coloradans. How to submit your house for inclusion on the map All private, residential holiday lights displays anywhere in Colorado are welcome, regardless which specific December holiday they might be celebrating. Our staff will review each submission to be sure it’s appropriate for inclusion and verify whether the location maps correctly, and may lightly edit any description text submitted. Be sure your photo shows your display in its best light: Take the picture after sunset but before full dark, and try to get your camera up in the air — reach up high, stand on a ladder or climb into a pickup bed to get a great angle. A thin, fresh blanket of snow doesn’t hurt at all. Now get those photos in! We all need plenty of lights to see on Christmas Eve before the obligatory Chinese-food dinner .

title: Colorado Supreme Court weighs case that ‘could impact the entire criminal justice system’
summary: A decade of criminal cases are called into question as the state’s highest court weighs constitutional protections for people convicted of crimes.
content: Earlier this year, a Weld County judge dismissed a case of sex assault on a child because DNA evidence for the case was first analyzed by Missy Woods, a state lab technician currently serving a prison sentence for falsifying records . The judge cited “outrageous government misconduct” by Woods and her employer, the Colorado Bureau of Investigation. Now this one aging case in northern Colorado could have ramifications for literally thousands of cases going back more than a decade in the state’s criminal justice system. In January, the Colorado Supreme Court will hear arguments from all of the sides on an issue that started with a lab technician who mishandled DNA and documentation for thousands of sexual assault swabs and a state cover-up that came to light in 2023. Woods pleaded guilty to four felonies and is in prison. Pool: Stephen Swofford/Denver Gazette Missy Woods is put into handcuffs in a Jefferson County courtroom after being sentenced a ten year prison sentence for cybercrime, and two six-year sentences for other crimes, which will be served simultaneously. Sept. 8, 2026. But the ramifications of her decade of misconduct, which lawyers argue spanned thousands of cases and were eventually documented by her employer, the Colorado Bureau of Investigation or CBI , in an exhaustive report before she was sentenced, continue to play out in Colorado’s state courts. In August, a Weld County District Court judge threw out a child sex assault case citing the doctrine of “outrageous government misconduct” committed by CBI and Woods because the suspect’s DNA was first analyzed by Woods. Attorneys for the suspect, Daniel Eatinger, argued that, because her analysis was the reason he was charged with the sex assault initially, it was impossible to unravel Woods’ misconduct in his case. Weld County Judge Vicente Vigil agreed — and he did not hold back “Ms Woods chose to become a cancer within the Colorado Bureau of Investigation,” he wrote. “And that agency chose first to ignore, then place a bandage on the tumor until it could no longer be hidden from public view.” But the county’s District Attorney Michael Rourke was stunned. His team said that while the case started with lab work conducted by Woods, re-tested DNA ultimately didn’t rely on any of Woods’ lab work and that work by others has not been called into question. Ultimately, Rourke asked the Colorado Supreme Court to intervene. Pool: Denver Post FILE – District Attorney Michael Rourke in Weld County District Court on October 13, 2020 in Greeley, Colo. In an email, Rourke said he is limited on what he can say in the open case now, but he did note that the state Supreme Court “has an incredibly important decision before it, which could impact the entire criminal justice system. “But truly at the heart of this controversy is a young victim who deserves her day in court. She and her need for justice cannot be lost in all of the legal wranglings,” he said. Prosecutors across the state are collectively concerned, said Jessica Dotter, who leads the Colorado District Attorney’s Council. That’s because the Weld County judge’s dismissal could affect thousands of other cases — even those with convictions and defendants in prisons. “This ruling, if upheld, would essentially mean that thousands of victims across Colorado would get punished for, you know, her wrongdoing, even if the wrongdoing had nothing to do with their cases,” Dotter said. “It would essentially set the precedent for judges across the state to do the same … even when there was no specific misconduct in that case. And that would have a negative impact on the victims.” Prosecutors wrote that to succeed on a claim of “outrageous misconduct, a defendant must show that his constitutional due process rights have been violated by the actions of government officials,” according to a friend of the court brief filed to the state Supreme Court on behalf of all 23 elected state district attorneys. They used italics as emphasis. “The doctrine exists to protect an individual’s due process rights,” the prosecutors wrote. “There is no precedent authorizing dismissal of a criminal case to punish an actor without first finding a concrete injury to the defendant.” Arguing the other side are defense attorneys and American Civil Liberties Union lawyers who say that CBI’s failure to disclose Woods’ misconduct for years — despite signs of problems as early as 2014 — means that for close to a decade the state violated constitutional protections for defendants. They argue that is because prosecutors are required to tell defense attorneys about all exculpatory evidence in criminal cases. This essentially means that prosecutors, law enforcement, and, yes, even the CBI, must furnish all evidence that supports a defendant’s innocence or creates reasonable doubt in cases. And because CBI didn’t disclose to anyone what was potentially going on for years — including prosecutors filing cases against thousands of defendants in cases ranging from sex assault to murder to theft — ACLU attorney Matthew Segal argues those defendants’ rights were violated. “Those rules cover not just instances of misconduct committed in the specific case at issue, but evidence that undermines someone’s credibility,” said Segal, co-director of the ACLU Foundation’s State Supreme Court Initiative. “And of course, the fact that Missy Woods was committing fraud is a fact that undermines her credibility in every case.” Segal said this entire argument has been overlooked in all of the discussions surrounding Woods’ misconduct and the potential fallout of Colorado’s criminal justice system. “It is a fundamentally important part of the criminal justice in America and in Colorado too,” he said. The Colorado Supreme Court has scheduled oral arguments for Jan. 13, 2027.

title: Personal data of 100K Coloradans breached in myColorado app hack
summary: State officials have yet to relaunch the app, which can include documents like passports, and vehicle registration.
content: About 100,000 Coloradans had their data temporarily exposed in a hack that forced the indefinite shutdown of the myColorado app on Nov. 18. On Wednesday, state officials said the hackers were able to access the “myDocuments” part of the app, which includes “PDFs and photographs of documents like passports, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards,” according to the app. Payment information was not involved. Staff roughly estimated that 100,000 people could be involved in the data breach, but expects to refine that number as it determines which documents were accessed. The Office of Information Technology anticipates that notifications will start being sent to affected users on Friday. The app has approximately 2.1 million users. While it is down, officials are urging users to carry their physical IDs while they travel. In addition to document storage, the app also offered ways to access various services , like driver’s license renewal, state benefit applications and Colorado Parks and Wildlife licenses. Those services remain available on their respective agency websites. Users who are worried their information might be compromised can take proactive steps to protect themselves. That includes changing passwords that match the one used on the myColorado app, freezing credit with all four bureaus, and documenting any unusual activity related to your identity.

title: A Colorado tradition: How to cut your own Christmas tree on public land
summary: Permits are available in many national forests and on public land across the state through December.
content: With standard live Christmas trees costing $50 or more, many Colorado families choose to cut their own on public lands, where permits range from $1 to $20. Both the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) have opened seasonal permits across the state, offering a fun outdoor activity that also helps with forest management. “Christmas tree cutting is a popular tradition,” said Reid Armstrong, public affairs officer for the Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forest and Pawnee National Grasslands. “Many families have been coming back for generations.” Armstrong said that the Sulphur and Canyon Lakes Ranger districts sell upwards of 10,000 permits per year, and attributed that to being near Fort Collins and the Front Range. The programs are also intended to support forest health by thinning smaller evergreen trees and encouraging more ecological diversity. First, find your spot The BLM offers individual Christmas tree permits for $1 per tree nationwide through Dec. 25 under its All Americans Outside initiative . The agency manages millions of acres of land in Colorado, including the Gunnison Gorge National Conservation Area and McInnis Canyons National Conservation Area. To cut a tree on BLM land, you must purchase a permit through a local field office and refer to official maps to determine where cutting is allowed. Carry your permit with you, and tag the tree immediately before bringing it home. Hart Van Denburg/CPR News Arapaho National Forest, west of Denver, on public land, has numerous Colorado Roadless Area parcels, including Bard Creek, a small part of which can be seen in the background, and Mt. Sniktau, a portion of which is in the foreground in this photo taken from Loveland Pass looking north. U.S. Forest Service permits work a little differently, and the cost is a bit higher. You must purchase a permit through your local ranger district, which can cost between $5 and $20. The South Platte Ranger District is popular for residents on the Front Range, while the Pikes Peak Ranger District is closest to Colorado Springs. “For a lot of people, it’s sort of like a family day trip where they combine it with other opportunities to enjoy the town near Red Feather Lakes or near Winter Park or Granby,” said Armstrong. In northwestern Colorado, the White River National Forest offers permits for $10 at district offices. If your fourth-grader is interested in cutting a tree, they can get a permit for free through the Every Kid Outdoors pass , which offers a voucher for a free USFS Christmas tree permit at participating forests. Each district opens permits on different dates — Pikes Peak is already open, and in South Platte, the first cutting day is Nov. 27, the Friday after Thanksgiving. Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests have permits available for $20. Refer to the public lands map for your area for specific spots to cut your tree. Officials generally encourage cutting in an area dense with pine . Find your tree Certain species, such as bristlecone pine, are off-limits in some areas, while species like pinyon pine and juniper are generally allowed. White spruce and fir trees are popular, though ponderosa pine and Douglas fir trees are restricted. Prohibited species vary by forest, so refer to the rules for your permit. There are also rules on how to cut them. On BLM land, never just cut off the top of a tall tree. Always cut the entire tree, and cut below the lowest live limb, leaving a stump no higher than 6 inches. Maximum height and trunk diameter rules vary by field office. Always clean up after you cut, and avoid damaging nearby trees. The USFS also has specific rules for diameters and size, so refer to your local office when you get your permit. Be safe Check road conditions — smaller roads on public lands are often closed in winter, and be aware of snow at high elevation. Officials recommend cutting a tree before it snows, making it easier to cut and load. “It definitely involves driving out, often into snowy areas, and having the right equipment and being willing to walk around and look for the right tree,” Armstrong said. “For some families, that tradition is enjoyable, and they keep coming back year after year.” Because tree cutting season on BLM land overlaps with some open hunting seasons, the agency recommends wearing blaze orange clothing, along with checking winter road closures and weather before heading out.

title: Author grapples with her own past in ‘Memoir of a Black Market Adoption’
summary: Patricia Knight Meyer recently won an award for the book from a Colorado-based book group.
content: Shortly after her birth, Patricia Knight Meyer was put into a car outside a Texas hospital. She was put up for adoption, but there was no paperwork or no birth certificate. In fact, there was nothing official about her adoption at all. It was part of a scam. In the early 1970s, the black market for adoptions was sprawling. It was known as the “Baby Scoop Era,” and Knight Meyer was a part of it. She’s uncovered a lot about her past as an adult and writes about it in her new book “Wonderland: Memoir of a Black Market Adoption.” The book recently won a 2026 EVVY Award in the category of memoir from the Colorado-based Collective of Independent Publishers and Authors. “The research that I did showed that 11,000 babies [nationwide] were sold on the black market the year I was placed alone, out of 175,000 children that were relinquished,” she told CPR News during November’s National Adoption Month. Here in Colorado, the law is different now than what she faced in Texas at the time. The state has taken steps to protect adoptees and their families and to prevent black market adoptions. For one, Colorado has a law that makes it illegal to exchange money or valuables in connection to an adoption, unless it’s through a licensed agency, county department or part of an official attorney fee. Only a court, county human services department or a licensed agency are able to place a child for adoption. And since 2016, adoptees born in Colorado can request their original birth certificate at age 18 without a court order. Knight Meyer says an attorney exploited her birth mom and her adoptive parents, who paid the attorney nearly $30,000 over many years for paperwork that was promised but never came. “Because in the 1960s, my father was a heavyset, large Hispanic man. My mother was a white woman. They were in a biracial marriage. He had a middle income. He was a meat inspector, and they really did not fit the stereotypical, perfect white…” Since they were being put at the back of the “I want a baby line,” Knight Meyer says a lot of times people would hire an attorney to try to speed up the process and go around the system. And when she finally found her birth mother decades later, even the birthday she had known and celebrated turned out to be different. In the book, Knight Meyer explores growing up without a legal identity and the kind of fantasies that so many adoptees create — known as “ghost kingdoms” — as they try to process their pasts and piece together and build stories about where they came from. “I felt like my own fabricated sense of ghost identity that I had created for myself shattered.” “I thought that I was going to know who I was better when I met [my birth mother], but because she wasn’t who I imagined I was going to meet, I felt like I knew myself even less. For Knight Meyer, meeting her birth mother was nothing like she’d imagined, and it shattered the identity she imagined for herself. “I didn’t see myself so much in my birth mother physically, but boy, I mean, there was so much about her that I recognized in myself. Unfortunately for her, it was a lot of the stuff that I didn’t like about myself that I saw in her,” she said. And meeting her birth father, who learned at the age of 69 that he had a daughter, turned out to be the joyful reunion she’d envisioned. Those two different experiences set her on a path to writing the book. “It’s not who you find, but that you find,” she said. Today, Knight Meyer advocates for adoption reform including rights for birth fathers.
